title: Scissors
wiki_lead:
Scissors or shears are hand-operated cutting tools that consist of a pair of pivoting blades whose sharpened edges slide firmly against and past each other when the handles (shank) on the opposite side of the pivot are squeezed shut. This causes the target material in between the blades to be divided by the combined effort of both cutting and shearing. Scissors are usually used for cutting thin materials such as paper, cardboard, metal foil, cloth, rope and wire, although a large variety of scissors/shears exist for specialized purposes, and their design details often dictate which is best for the intended job. 
While all scissors largely follow the same working principle, heavy-duty scissors intended for cutting tough materials tend to be called shears instead of scissors (e.g. pruning shears and grass shears), and some larger, two-handed implements are called trimmers instead (e.g. hedge trimmer). Choosing the optimal type of scissors/shears is crucial, as otherwise it can cause unwanted damage to the target material and/or the instrument itself. For example, hair-cutting shears and kitchen shears are functionally equivalent scissors, but hair-cutting shears have specific blade angles ideal for cutting heaped bundles of hair, and using the incorrect type of scissors will result in increased damage or split ends, or both, by breaking the hair; kitchen shears, also known as kitchen scissors, are intended for cutting and trimming tough food materials such as meat, tendon and bones. Surgical scissors, used to divide tissues and trim/reshape implants during surgical operations, have an even greater variety to deal with different anatomical and procedural circumstances. 
Most scissors have a ringed handle to allow readily opening for repeated cutting, and some even have spring between the shanks to assist opening (especially for shears with straight handle). While historically inexpensive, mass-produced scissors often have bare metal handles, modern scissors are often designed ergonomically with composite thermoplastic and rubber covering on handles, which are more comfortable for the hand.

Terminology
The noun scissors is treated as a plural noun and therefore takes a plural verb (e.g., these scissors are). Alternatively, the tool is referred to by the singular phrase a pair of scissors. In everyday language, the words shears and snips are used to describe similar instruments that are larger in size and for heavier cutting. Archaeologists distinguish between shears with a bow (the older, simpler technology) and scissors with a pivot (the newer, more difficult technology).


History

In Europe, shears with a bow appear around 1000 BCE. At that time, they seem to have been rare because there were few common tasks which they did better than a knife. Hair could be trimmed with a razor and cloth was woven to shape. Gradually many Europeans came to shear their sheep rather than plucking or combing the wool from the animal, and this task required shears or scissors. Scissors with a pivot became common in north-west Europe around the 13th and 14th century CE and were useful for the increasingly elaborate tailoring of the period. Scissors offer the precision of a knife with the protection for the underlying surface of shears. By the 15th century, large scissors like modern tin snips were also used to cut iron and steel in trades such as armouring. Fastening one arm to a block of wood created powerful lever action. However, making long straight blades which twist just enough to meet perfectly as the handles are squeezed is difficult, so simple bow shears remained common.  One dealer estimates that a pair of scissors blades are at least ten times as much work as a knife.

grok_lead: Scissors are hand-operated shearing tools consisting of two pivoted blades that slide against each other when the handles are squeezed together, enabling precise cutting of materials such as paper, cloth, thread, food, hair, and thin metals. The term "scissors" originates from the late 14th-century Old French cisoires, meaning "shears," which derives from the Vulgar Latin cÄ«sÅria and ultimately from the Latin caedere, "to cut," reflecting the tool's fundamental purpose. The earliest known precursors to modern scissors, known as spring scissors, date back to around 3000â4000 years ago in ancient Mesopotamia, with well-documented U-shaped bronze tools with spring-like blades used for cutting tasks without a pivot mechanism appearing around 1500 BCE in ancient Egypt. The Romans developed the cross-bladed, pivoted design around 100 CE, using iron blades that more closely resemble contemporary scissors, though these were initially considered a form of shears for larger cuts. By the early 6th century CE, the modern pivot-jointed scissors were in use in Europe, as described by Isidore of Seville, and in 1761, English cutler Robert Hinchliffe pioneered the production of scissors from cast steel, improving durability and sharpness for widespread adoption. Scissors vary widely in design to suit specific applications, with distinctions based on blade length âtypically those under 15 cm (6 inches) are classified as scissors, while longer ones are shearsâand specialized features like serrated edges or rounded tips. Common types include tailoring scissors for fabric, surgical scissors for medical procedures, pinking shears for zigzag cuts to prevent fraying, safety scissors with blunt tips for children, and heavy-duty shears like bolt cutters for metal. Their versatility has made them indispensable in households, industries, and professions ranging from crafting and grooming to surgery and manufacturing, where ergonomic handles and high-quality steel enhance precision and reduce fatigue.
